doping.short: Adding a tiny, controlled amount of another element to a pure semiconductor to give it spare electrons (n-type) or spare holes (p-type).

n-type.short: Silicon doped with an element such as phosphorus, whose atoms each give up one extra electron. Electrons are the majority carriers.

p-type.short: Silicon doped with an element such as boron, whose atoms each accept an electron and leave a hole behind. Holes are the majority carriers.

hole.short: The gap left where an electron is missing from a bond. It moves through the crystal like a positive charge.

electron-hole-pair.short: A free electron and the hole it left behind, created together when a photon with enough energy is absorbed.

pn-junction.short: The boundary inside one crystal where p-type silicon meets n-type silicon. Its built-in electric field separates light-made electrons and holes.

depletion-region.short: The thin layer around a p-n junction that has been emptied of free carriers, leaving fixed charged atoms that set up an electric field.

built-in-potential.short: The voltage step across a p-n junction in the dark, created by the fixed charges in the depletion region. About 0.6 to 0.9 V in silicon.

diffusion.short: Carriers spreading from where they are crowded to where they are scarce, just by random motion.

drift.short: Carriers moving because an electric field pushes them: electrons against the field, holes along it.

recombination.short: A free electron falling back into a hole. The pair's energy is lost as heat or light and can no longer drive a current.

intrinsic-carrier-density.short: How many free electrons (and equally many holes) pure, undoped silicon has from heat alone: about 10¹⁰ per cubic centimetre at room temperature.

iv-curve.short: A graph of the current a solar cell delivers against its voltage, from short circuit to open circuit.

short-circuit-current.short: The current a cell delivers when its terminals are wired straight together, so the voltage is zero. It grows in proportion to the light.

open-circuit-voltage.short: The voltage across a cell when nothing is connected and no current flows. About 0.6 to 0.75 V for silicon cells.

maximum-power-point.short: The point on the I-V curve where current × voltage is largest. Inverters keep panels there by tracking it (MPPT).

fill-factor.short: The maximum power divided by Voc × Isc. It says how square the I-V curve is; good silicon cells reach about 0.8 or more.

conversion-efficiency.short: The share of the sunlight power landing on a cell that comes out as electrical power, measured at standard test conditions.

standard-test-conditions.short: The agreed lab conditions for rating solar cells: 1000 W/m² of light with the AM1.5 spectrum and a cell temperature of 25 °C.

series-resistance.short: Resistance in the path current must travel: the silicon itself, the metal fingers and the contacts. It tilts the right side of the I-V curve.

shunt-resistance.short: A leakage path that lets current sneak around the junction instead of going to the load. Low values tilt the flat top of the I-V curve.

ideality-factor.short: A number, usually between 1 and 2, that says how closely a diode follows the ideal diode law. Higher values mean more recombination in the junction and a rounder I-V curve.

saturation-current.short: The tiny leakage current of a diode in the dark, set by recombination. The smaller it is, the higher the cell's voltage.
